abstract: The European eel (Anguilla anguilla) is critically endangered and subject to regulations requiring safe passage at migratory barriers and water intakes, but remediation must be prioritised to maximise conservation benefits. This study developed a novel prioritisation framework for both upstream and downstream eel passage remediation in heavily modified and fragmented pumped river systems. Catchment area (habitat quantity), distance from the tidal limit and numbers of migration barriers downstream were used as baseline geospatial metrics for bi-directional passage data. Following this, eel presence/absence data was incorporated to separate sites into upstream and downstream passage prioritisations, with site-specific hydrological connectivity (downstream) and fish community richness (upstream) data further refining rankings. Prioritisation rankings were compared iteratively to assess the influence of combining variables. Eel presence/absence data substantially altered downstream passage priorities relative to geospatial metrics alone, with a maximum rank change of 96 and eleven sites changing by 50 or more places. For downstream passage, hydrological connectivity resulted in significant re-ranking of priorities. For upstream passage, including fish species richness as an indicator for habitat quality caused notable re-ranking of sites compared with geospatial metrics alone. The results demonstrate that prioritisation based solely on geospatial metrics risks overlooking important sites and, consequently, directing resources towards areas with limited conservation potential. The iterative, flexible framework presented in this study provides a transparent and transferable approach for informing eel passage investment within heavily modified drainage systems and could be adapted to other landscapes where anguillid eels are conservation priorities.
